title: Rent vs Buy a Home: The Full Math Nobody Shows You
description:
Rent vs buy a home: we run the full math for a median-priced US house at today's mortgage rates, including property tax, insurance, repairs, closing and selling costs, and what your down payment could earn if you rented instead. Buying can take 5 years to beat renting, or 20: with our assumptions it's about 20 at the median sale price, and the price-to-rent ratio, the number most buyers never check, can cut that to 5 or push it past 30. Plus a 5-question checklist.

Our example: $421,900 home (NAR median single-family, Oct 2026), $2,243/month rent (Zillow typical single-family asking rent, Oct 2026), 20% down, 30-year fixed at 7.28% (Freddie Mac, Nov 19, 2026), property tax 0.9% a year (ATTOM), insurance $2,564 a year (NerdWallet).
Assumptions (ours, not predictions): 3% to buy, 6% to sell, repairs 1% of value a year (a rule of thumb), home prices, rent and costs grow 3% a year, investments earn 6% a year, whoever spends less each month invests the difference, 15% tax on investment gains when cashed out, the buyers are a married couple, so the home's gain is tax-free up to $500,000 and 15% above that (IRS exclusion; single owners: $250,000, which our example passes in year 19, so a single owner breaks even about a year later, in year 22, and leads by less at year 30), no mortgage-interest deduction (it only helps if you itemize), no renters insurance. The NAR price is a median sale price and the Zillow rent a typical asking rent, so they are not the exact same homes. Real returns, prices and rents vary and can be negative. Zillow's break-even estimates use Zillow's own model and inputs, including its lower typical home value ($364,812 in October 2026, which includes condos); at that value our model gives about 9 years.

Sources:
- National Association of Realtors, Existing-Home Sales Decreased 5.5% in October (Nov 12, 2026): https://www.nar.realtor/newsroom/existing-home-sales-decreased-5-5-percent-october-nar-report
- Zillow, A house doesn't have to mean a mortgage: Renting requires $14K less income than buying (Nov 12, 2026; typical single-family rent, Zillow Observed Rent Index): https://s25.q4cdn.com/975009107/files/doc_news/A-house-doesnt-have-to-mean-a-mortgage-Renting-requires-14K-less-income-than-buying-2026.pdf
- Zillow, Rent or buy: How long it takes for buying a home to pay off in each metro (Jun 4, 2026): https://zillow.mediaroom.com/2026-06-04-Rent-or-buy-How-long-it-takes-for-buying-a-home-to-pay-off-in-each-metro
- Zillow, Newly pending listings fell 17% in October (Nov 2026; typical home value, ZHVI): https://s25.q4cdn.com/975009107/files/doc_news/Newly-pending-listings-fell-17-in-October-the-biggest-year-over-year-drop-since-2023-2026.pdf
- Freddie Mac, Primary Mortgage Market Survey (Nov 19, 2026 and Jun 4, 2026): https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms
- ATTOM, 2025 property tax analysis (Apr 9, 2026): https://www.attomdata.com/news/market-trends/home-sales-prices/2025-annual-tax-report
- NerdWallet, Home insurance pricing report 2026 (Oct 2, 2026): https://www.nerdwallet.com/insurance/homeowners/home-insurance-pricing-report-2026

For education only. Not financial advice. Past results don't guarantee future returns.

scenes.say: An American home can take five years to beat renting, or twenty, at today's mortgage rates. It depends on a few numbers, and the biggest one most buyers never check.

visual.label: years for buying to beat renting
visual.sub: same rent, different price · Nov 19, 2026 rate · our model

scenes.say: Same rent. At the median sale price, about twenty years. At a cheaper price, about five. Most rent versus buy advice skips this part.
So we'll run the full math nobody shows you: the mortgage, property tax, insurance, repairs, the fees to buy and sell, and what your down payment could have earned instead.

visual.title: The full math
items: Fees to buy and to sell
What your cash could earn instead

scenes.say: By the end, you'll know that one number for your own city, and you'll have a five-question checklist to use before you sign anything.

visual.title: Rent vs Buy
visual.sub: the full math, and a checklist

scenes.say: Chapter one. The two homes.

We'll use real, current US numbers. In October, the median existing single-family home sold for four hundred twenty-one thousand nine hundred dollars, according to the National Association of Realtors.

Renting a single-family home? Zillow says the typical asking rent in October was two thousand two hundred forty-three dollars a month, up three point two percent in a year. A sale price and an asking rent aren't the exact same homes, but they're a fair national match.
Our buyer puts twenty percent down, about eighty-four thousand dollars, and borrows the rest, about three hundred thirty-seven and a half thousand, on a thirty-year fixed mortgage.
The rate: Freddie Mac's weekly survey put the average thirty-year fixed rate at seven point two eight percent on November nineteenth. A year earlier, it was six point two six.
On top of the down payment come closing costs. Redfin says buyers usually pay two to five percent of the price. We'll use three percent: almost thirteen thousand dollars.

visual.label: closing costs to buy (3%, our assumption)

scenes.say: So the buyer needs about ninety-seven thousand dollars in cash on day one. The renter keeps that money and invests it. Now, what does owning really cost each month? More than the mortgage.
Chapter two. The monthly bill.
The mortgage payment, principal plus interest, is about two thousand three hundred nine dollars a month, fixed for thirty years.

Then property tax. The data firm Attom puts the average effective rate on US single-family homes at about zero point nine percent of the value a year. Here, that's about three hundred sixteen dollars a month.
Home insurance: NerdWallet's typical US premium in early twenty twenty-six was two thousand five hundred sixty-four dollars a year. About two hundred fourteen a month, and far more in some states.

visual.title: Home insurance
visual.label: typical US premium · ≈ $214 a month · NerdWallet, 2026

scenes.say: And repairs. A common rule of thumb says set aside about one percent of the home's value every year. It's a rough guide, not data: older homes can need more. Here, about three hundred fifty a month.

visual.text:
Budget about 1% of
the home's value a year
visual.source: rule of thumb for repairs · here ≈ $352 a month

scenes.say: Add it up, and owning costs about three thousand one hundred ninety dollars a month. Renting the same kind of home: two thousand two hundred forty-three.
That's about nine hundred fifty dollars a month more to own. But that comparison is unfair to the buyer, because part of that payment isn't a cost at all.

lines.text: but is it all a cost?

scenes.say: Chapter three. Money gone, money kept.

In year one, the buyer pays the bank about twenty-seven thousand seven hundred dollars. About twenty-four and a half thousand of it is interest. Only about three thousand two hundred pays down the loan.
That loan payoff is savings. It's still yours. So the honest comparison is the money that's gone for good: interest, tax, insurance and repairs. These are often called unrecoverable costs.
Plus one that's easy to miss: that ninety-seven thousand dollars of cash. Invested at six percent a year, our assumption, it could have earned about five thousand eight hundred dollars in year one.

visual.title: What the cash could have earned
visual.label: $97,037 × 6% a year, in year one

scenes.say: Add it all up, and the buyer's money that's gone is about three thousand four hundred dollars a month. The renter's rent is gone too: two thousand two hundred forty-three.

visual.title: Money gone for good, per month (year one)

scenes.say: Now the buyer's big advantage: the house can grow in value. At an assumed three percent a year, that's about twelve thousand seven hundred dollars in year one. But prices don't always rise. Over the past year, the national median rose just zero point four percent.

Take that growth off, and owning costs about two thousand three hundred fifty a month, against two thousand two hundred forty-three for renting. Close. So why could break-even take twenty years? Two big fees: one to get in, one to get out.

visual.title: Money gone, minus price growth (per month)

scenes.say: Chapter four. The fees to get in and out.

visual.title: The fees to get in and out

scenes.say: Getting in costs those closing costs. Getting out costs more. In one twenty twenty-six survey, agent commissions alone averaged about five and a half percent of the sale price. We assume six percent in total to sell.

visual.title: Fees as a share of the home price
visual.note: Our assumptions · Redfin: 2–5% to buy · Clever (2026): agent fees avg 5.46%

scenes.say: Sell after five years, and the house might be worth about four hundred eighty-nine thousand dollars. Six percent of that is about twenty-nine thousand. Add the thirteen thousand to buy, and that's about forty-two thousand dollars in fees.

visual.title: Buy now, sell in 5 years
visual.label: $12.7K to buy + $29.3K to sell, if the home is worth $489K

scenes.say: To come out ahead, the buyer has to win those fees back, through rising prices and paying down the loan, before the renter's investments pull too far ahead.
Fees come first. Time pays them back, slowly. So when does the buyer actually catch up? Let's run all thirty years.

visual.text:
Fees come first.
Time pays them back.

scenes.say: Chapter five. The break-even year.

Here are the rules. Each month, whoever spends less invests the difference at six percent. Rent, home prices, tax, insurance and repairs all rise three percent a year. We skip renters insurance, a small cost. These are assumptions, not predictions.

visual.title: The rules (our assumptions)
items: Whoever spends less invests the gap at 6%
Rent and home prices rise 3% a year

scenes.say: When we compare, the renter pays fifteen percent tax on investment gains, a typical US rate on long-term gains. The buyer's home profit is tax-free only within the IRS exclusion: up to two hundred fifty thousand dollars, or five hundred thousand for a married couple. Our example is a married couple, so it stays within that until almost the end. A single owner would pass the limit around year nineteen, and break even about a year later. And the buyer pays the six percent to sell.

items.label: tax on investment gains
items.sub: IRS: at most 15% for most people

scenes.say: Here's how far ahead the renter would be if both cashed out. The renter starts ahead, with all that cash invested. The buyer starts behind, because of the fees. Then the gap slowly shrinks.

visual.title: Renter's lead if both cashed out
visual.note: our model · assumptions above · not a prediction

scenes.say: After five years, the renter is about forty-three thousand dollars ahead. After ten, still about forty-one thousand ahead.
Then, around year twenty, the lines cross. Rent keeps rising every year, while the mortgage payment stays fixed. By then, the rent costs more than owning each month, and the buyer pulls ahead.
By year thirty, with the mortgage paid off, the buyer is ahead by about a hundred and twenty-six thousand dollars.

visual.label: buyer ahead after 30 years
visual.sub: our model · assumed 3% price growth, 6% returns

scenes.say: But only if the renter really invests the difference, every month, for decades. Many people don't. A mortgage forces you to save. Renting doesn't. So is buying a bad deal? Not necessarily. Watch what happens when we change one number.

visual.text:
Renting wins only if you
invest the difference.

scenes.say: Chapter six. Change one number.

That number is the price-to-rent ratio. Divide the home's price by a full year of rent. Here, four hundred twenty-one thousand nine hundred, divided by about twenty-seven thousand, is about fifteen point seven.

lines.text: years of rent to buy the home

scenes.say: Keep the same rent, and change only the price. At twelve times a year's rent, break-even drops to about five years. At ten times, about three. At fourteen, about ten. And at eighteen, the buyer doesn't catch up within thirty years.

Real cities show the same spread. Zillow's own model put the national break-even at about six years in June. It uses Zillow's lower typical home value and its own assumptions. Plug that value into our model, and we get about nine years at today's rate. In Columbus, Ohio, about four. In San Diego, over twenty-three. In San Francisco and San Jose, never within thirty years.

visual.title: Zillow: years for buying to pay off (June 2026)
visual.note: Zillow's model and inputs differ from ours

scenes.say: Other dials matter too. A six percent mortgage rate: about nine years. Home prices rising four percent a year: about ten. Only two percent: about thirty. Investments earning five percent: about fourteen. Earning seven: the renter stays ahead for over thirty years.

visual.title: Change one thing (everything else the same)

scenes.say: From three years to more than thirty, from small changes. So anyone who says renting is throwing money away, or that buying is always a trap, is skipping the math. How do you find your own answer? Five questions.

visual.title: Renting vs buying
visual.label: "Renting is throwing money away" skips the math

scenes.say: Chapter seven. Your checklist.

One: how long will you stay? Two: what's the price-to-rent ratio where you live? Three: what's the full monthly cost, not just the mortgage? Four: can you afford the fees to buy and to sell? Five: if you rent, will you really invest the difference?

visual.title: Rent or buy: 5 questions
items: Price ÷ yearly rent where you live?
Full monthly cost, not just the mortgage?
Can you afford the fees to buy and sell?

scenes.say: For question one: short stays usually favor renting, because the fees come first. With our numbers, selling after five years leaves the buyer about forty-three thousand dollars behind.

For question three, use the same list we did: interest, tax, insurance, about one percent for repairs, and what your cash could earn. Take off the price growth you expect, then compare that with the rent.
And remember what the math leaves out. Owning gives you stability and control over your home. Renting gives you flexibility, and the landlord pays for the new roof. Only you can put a price on those.

right.label: Renting
right.sub: easy to move, no roof bills

scenes.say: Rent versus buy isn't a moral question. It's a math question, and a life question. How long you stay and your local prices decide a lot of it. Run your own numbers before you sign anything.

visual.title: Run your own numbers
visual.label: how long you stay + local prices decide a lot
